Damian Betebenner & Adam VanIwaarden
Center for Assessment

January 29th, 2026

SGP Background
• An SGP is a conditional probability:
SGP ≡ 100 ⋅ Pr(Current Score or Less | Prior Score(s))
• For example, an SGP of 90 implies that the probability of
observing the current score or less given the prior score(s) is
• Equivalently, an SGP of 90 implies that the probability of
observing the current score or higher given the prior(s) is 0.1.
• SGPs are calculated using non-parametric (b-spline based)
quantile regression.

SGP: Scale agnosticism
• SGPs, being norm-referenced, are, in general, immune to assessment
transitions:
• As long as all students take the “same” assessment at the “same”
time, we can calculate growth-norms associated with those students.
• In addition, the analytic methodology behind SGP calculation is designed
to be invariant to mono-tone transformations of scale.
• In theory, if there is a mono-tone transformation of scale between
two assessments, then SGPs will be invariant to that transformation.
• SGPs have been successfully calculated across numerous assessment
transitions (state transition to PARCC and SBAC, for example)

SGP: Properties and Goodness-of-Fit
• Given that SGPs are, by definition, conditional probabilities,
they are independent (i.e., uncorrelated) with the conditioning
variable - prior score(s).
• Percentiles, by definition are uniformly distributed. One way to
test whether the model fits the data is to test against
uniformity.
• Goodness-of-Fit plots exported as part of the SGP run help see
to what extent observed SGPs deviate from the theoretic
expectation.

Several Issues to Consider
• Based upon my examination of these cases, there isn’t an issue
with “calculations”. All the SGP calculations are as expected.
• However, there are other issues that are problematic:
• The reporting scale is not a strictly mono-tone transformation
of the theta scale (many theta scores get mapped to 850).
Thus, same scale score trajectories lead to different SGPs.
• The multi-variate density is, obviously, extremely sparse at the
extremes, so SGP accuracy and precision are questionable.

Several Issues to Consider
• Issues with ceiling effects on the test have long been an issue in SGP calculation.
• Several states have adopted the policy of just assigning an SGP of 99 to any
student getting a perfect score (e.g., 850).
• That may obviate the issue at the HOSS, however, there are likely issues near
the HOSS that aren’t “corrected”.
• When an over-preponderance of students are assigned the HOSS, then low SGPs
can result (indicating, correctly, the the probability of having a perfect current
score is not “rare” given perfect prior scores)
• However, that mathematical explanation does not translate into the correct
message for a parent.

Summary
• At the ceiling of the IAR, there are issues with the accuracy and precision of the SGPs.
• There are two intersecting issues:
• Use of theta values for SGP calculation
• Reporting of SGPs with scale scores
• Probably the best way to over come these issues (as best they can from an analytic
perspective) is:
• Calculate SGPs using scaled scores (in addition to thetas just to have those too).
• Investigate and deal with any emerging ceiling issues (lots of 850s in the analysis)
by possibly assigning all students a 99.
• More broadly, the question is, “What score decline at the top of the scale should we
be comfortable signaling is worrisome?”
